# Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta (MN 77 (PTS MN ii 1))
**ID:** MN 77 (PTS MN ii 1)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Longer Discourse with Sakuludāyī
**PTS:** MN ii 1

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāsakuludāyi Sutta* ("The Longer Discourse with Sakuludāyī", MN 77; PTS MN ii 1–22) records an exchange between the Buddha and the wanderer Sakuludāyin [SuttaCentral; Emmanuel 2013]. While Sakuludāyin observes that the disciples of the six renowned contemporary teachers—each the head of an order revered by many—frequently quarrel with their leaders, the Buddha's followers revere and honour him with authentic devotion [Aston 2004; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; SuttaCentral]. The Buddha clarifies that he is not respected merely for asceticism or austere eating habits, contrasting his occasional consumption of full bowls of food with disciples who practice strict frugality [Anālayo 2017]; rather, disciples venerate him for five true qualities: higher morality, profound wisdom, vision of knowledge, and his detailed instruction on the spiritual path that accommodates diverse ascetic and meditative practices [Emmanuel 2013; Meisig 2010].
Doctrinally, the sutta provides an extensive survey of meditative frameworks, enumerating sixty-eight practices and attainments [Kamalashila 2012]. These include the thirty-seven aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*) [Aston 2004], the ten *kasiṇa* bases [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995], the eight bases of transcendence (*abhibhāyatana*), and the eight liberations (*aṭṭha-vimokkhā*) [Hung 2010; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. It also details the mastery of psychic powers, such as producing a mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) endowed with faculties [Sorensen 2013]. In this context, it is the only sutta outside the *Dīgha Nikāya* to employ the "snake slough" pericope to illustrate the extraction of the mind-made body from the physical body [Radich 2007]. Additionally, it uses the term *pāramippatta* in reference to senior disciples attaining the culmination of spiritual practice [Appleton 2010].
A full parallel to the sutta is preserved in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 207) [SuttaCentral]. Comparative analysis shows that the elaborate doctrinal exposition under the fifth praiseworthy quality is absent in MĀ 207, suggesting that this portion of MN 77 represents a later expansion that incorporated commentarial expositions [Meisig 2010]. Other parallels and shared sections identified by SuttaCentral include DN 10, DN 15, DN 16, DN 33, DN 34, MN 137, and various sets in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (e.g., AN 10.29, AN 8.65–66) [SuttaCentral]. Automatically computed text reuse by DharmaNexus corroborates extensive formulaic sharing across Pali texts, especially with the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Sāmaññaphala Sutta* (DN 2), *Subha Sutta* (DN 10), and *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33), as well as Sanskrit alignments with the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, *Daśabalasūtra*, and *Saṅgītisūtra* [DharmaNexus].
